4145755.title: Clouds Hill
4145755.extract: Clouds Hill is an isolated early 19th-century cottage near Wareham in the county of Dorset in South West England. It is the former home of T. E. Lawrence. The cottage is a Grade II* listed building and is owned by the National Trust.

main.*:
{{hatnote|For the estate in Warwick, Rhode Island, see [[Clouds Hill (Warwick, Rhode Island)]].}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Use British English|date=February 2023}} {{Infobox building | name = Clouds Hill | image = Clouds Hill, Bovington.jpg | caption = The front of Clouds Hill in 2013 | pushpin_map = United Kingdom Dorset | map_caption = Location within Dorset | architectural_style = | building_type = Cottage | coordinates = {{coord|50.7176|-2.2510|type:landmark_region:GB|display=inline,title}} | location = near [[Wareham, Dorset|Wareham]], [[Dorset]] | completion_date = 19th century | owner = [[National Trust]] | website = https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clouds-hill }} '''Clouds Hill''' is an isolated early 19th-century cottage near [[Wareham, Dorset|Wareham]] in the county of [[Dorset]] in [[South West England]]. It is the former home of [[T. E. Lawrence]]. The cottage is a [[Grade II* listed building]] and is owned by the [[National Trust]]. ==History== [[File:Engraving over doorway, Clouds Hill, Dorset - geograph.org.uk - 587818.jpg|thumb|The carving of ''οὐ φροντὶς'' over the doorway]] The small building has colourwashed brick walls and a tiled roof. It was probably built as a forester's or labourer's [[cottage]] in 1808 but was largely reconstructed in 1922-34 by [[T. E. Lawrence]] ("Lawrence of Arabia") for himself. The lintel over the door bears a Greek inscription {{lang|grc|[[Hippocleides|οὐ φροντὶς]]}} ("why worry"). The site was in the parish of [[Turners Puddle]] in [[Purbeck District]]. As "Clouds Hill (Lawrence of Arabia's Cottage)", it is now a [[Grade II* listed building]]; it was upgraded from Grade II in 2015.{{National Heritage List for England| num=1120423 |desc=Clouds Hill (Lawrence of Arabia's Cottage)|grade=II* |accessdate=26 April 2018}} Lawrence first rented the cottage in 1923 while stationed at nearby [[Bovington Camp]] with the [[Royal Tank Regiment|Tank Corps]].{{cite book |title=Dorset |first=John |last=Hyams |publisher=B. T. Batsford Ltd |pages=68–9 |year=1970 |isbn=0-7134-0066-8}}{{cite book |title=Dorset Villages |first=Roland |last=Gant |publisher=Robert Hale Ltd |year=1980 |page=194 |isbn=0-7091-8135-3}} He made it habitable with the help of a friend, then bought it in 1925 and used it as a holiday home. He described it as an earthly paradise and wrote "Nothing in Clouds Hill is to be a care upon the world. While I have it there shall be nothing exquisite or unique in it. Nothing to anchor me."{{cite news |last1=Kennedy |first1=Maeve |title=TE Lawrence's Dorset cottage given extra protection |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2015/dec/15/te-lawrence-dorset-cottage-clouds-hill-listed-status |access-date=15 December 2015 |publisher=The Guardian Newspaper}} The cottage had no electric lights and three living rooms, described as an eating room, book room and music room. For heat insulation Lawrence had the eating room lined with [[asbestos]] that was covered in aluminium foil, and he kept his food under [[bell jar]]s; a ship’s [[porthole]], from the broken-up [[HMS Tiger (1913)|HMS ''Tiger'']], was installed in 1935. In the book room he installed a large leather [[Divan (furniture)|divan]], and in the music room above it he had his [[Phonograph|gramophone]] "with a huge amplifier horn", a leather sofa and chair. In a 1934 letter to [[Francis Rodd, 2nd Baron Rennell|Francis Rodd]], Lawrence (who had changed his surname to Shaw) described his home thus:{{cite web |title=T. E. Lawrence to The Hon. Francis Rodd |url=http://www.telstudies.org/writings/letters/1934/341123_f_rodd.shtml |website=Telstudies.org |access-date=26 February 2021}}
"The cottage has two rooms, one, upstairs, for music (a gramophone and [[Phonograph record|records]]) and one downstairs for books. There is a bath in a demi-cupboard. For food one goes a mile, to Bovington (near the Tank Corps Depot) and at sleep time I take a great sleeping bag... and spread it on what seems the nicest floor... The cottage looks simple outside, and does no hurt to its setting which is twenty miles of broken heath and a river valley filled with rhododendrons run wild. I think everything, inside and outside my place, approaches perfection... Yours ever, T. E. Shaw"
In 1935 Lawrence left the [[Royal Air Force]] and lived at Clouds Hill. A few weeks later, at the age of 46, he suffered injuries in a motorcycle accident close to the cottage, and died in the Bovington Camp hospital on 19 May 1935. The following year, his heir, his brother [[A. W. Lawrence]], gave Clouds Hill to the National Trust. It is now a museum, dedicated to Lawrence. It is open to visitors from March to the beginning of October. The cottage remains largely as Lawrence left it at his death. It features an exhibition detailing Lawrence's life, and most of his original furniture and possessions. The cottage reflects his complex personality and links to the [[Middle East]]. In it is displayed a painting by [[Henry Scott Tuke]] of a soldier cadet, possibly Lawrence, at Newporth Beach.{{cite web |title=A Soldier (possibly T. E. Lawrence) at Newporth Beach, near Falmouth |url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/628439 |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=2 January 2025}} The circular Lawrence of Arabia Trail starts and finishes at Bovington's [[The Tank Museum]], taking in Clouds Hill and the churchyard of [[St Nicholas, Moreton|St Nicholas' Church]] in [[Moreton, Dorset|Moreton]], where Lawrence is buried.{{cite web |title=Lawrence of Arabia Trail |url=https://www.dorsetcouncil.gov.uk/w/lawrence-of-arabia-trail?p_l_back_url=%2Fsearch%3Fq%3Dlawrence%2Btrail |publisher=[[Dorset Council (UK)|Dorset Council]] |access-date=2 January 2025}} ==Sleeping bags== [[File:CloudsHill3.jpg|thumb|The rear of the cottage]] Lawrence reserved a [[sleeping bag]] for visitors who stayed overnight. His own sleeping bag was marked ''meum'' ('mine' in [[Latin]]) and the bag for a guest, ''tuum'' ('yours'). According to [[Jeremy Wilson]], Lawrence's biographer, ''tuum''{{'}}s occupants included [[George Bernard Shaw]], [[E. M. Forster]] and [[Robert Graves]]. In 1965 the visitor's bag was stolen. Its disappearance coincided with the release of the film ''[[Lawrence of Arabia (film)|Lawrence of Arabia]]'' and it was thought the theft could have been inspired by the publicity generated by the film. In 2001, the sleeping bag was returned anonymously from Belgium.{{Cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/this-britain/lawrence-of-arabias-stolen-sleeping-bag-is-posted-home-after-36-years-680858.html|title=Lawrence of Arabia's stolen sleeping bag is posted home after 36 years|last=Whitney|first=Anna|date=9 April 2001|website=The Independent|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101106031832/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/this-britain/lawrence-of-arabias-stolen-sleeping-bag-is-posted-home-after-36-years-680858.html|archive-date=6 November 2010|url-status=dead|access-date=25 April 2019}} == Gallery == The Music Room, Clouds Hill.jpg|The Music Room The Bunk Rom, Clouds Hill.jpg|The Bunk Room CloudsHill2.jpg|The thatched garage of Clouds Hill, built in 1930, containing an exhibition on the life of Lawrence ==See also== * [[Writer's home]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Clouds Hill}} *[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/clouds-hill Clouds Hill information at the National Trust] [[Category:Biographical museums in Dorset]] [[Category:Cottages in Dorset]] [[Category:Grade II* listed buildings in Dorset]] [[Category:Grade II* listed houses]] [[Category:Historic house museums in Dorset]] [[Category:Literary museums in England]] [[Category:National Trust properties in Dorset]] [[Category:T. 22017946.title: Cerne Abbas Giant
22017946.extract:
The Cerne Abbas Giant, or Cerne Giant, is a hill figure near the village of Cerne Abbas, in Dorset, England. It is currently owned by the National Trust, and listed as a scheduled monument of England. Measuring 55 metres (180 ft) in length, the hill figure depicts a bald, nude male with a prominent erection, holding his left hand out to the side and wielding a large club in his right hand. Like many other hill figures, the Cerne Giant is formed by shallow trenches cut into the turf and backfilled with chalk rubble.
The origin and age of the figure are unclear, and archaeological evidence suggests that parts of it have been lost, altered, or added, over time; the earliest written record dates to the late 17th century. Early antiquarians associated it, albeit on little evidence, with a Saxon deity, while other scholars sought to identify it with a Romano-British figure of Hercules (or some syncretisation of the two). The lack of earlier descriptions, along with information given to the 18th-century antiquarian John Hutchins, has led some scholars to conclude it dates from the 17th century. Conversely, recent optically stimulated luminescence testing has suggested an origin between the years 700 CE and 1110 CE, possibly close to the 10th-century date of the founding of nearby Cerne Abbey.
Regardless of its age, the Cerne Giant has become an important part of local culture and folklore, which often associates it with fertility. It is one of England's best-known hill figures and is a visitor attraction in the region.
The Cerne Giant is one of two major extant human hill figures in England, the other being the Long Man of Wilmington, near Wilmington, East Sussex, which is also a scheduled monument.

The '''Cerne Abbas Giant''', or '''Cerne Giant''', is a [[hill figure]] near the village of [[Cerne Abbas]], in [[Dorset]], England. It is currently owned by the [[National Trust]], and listed as a [[scheduled monument]] of England. Measuring {{convert|55|m}} in length, the hill figure depicts a bald, [[nude]] male with a prominent [[erection]], holding his left hand out to the side and wielding a large club in his right hand. Like many other hill figures, the Cerne Giant is formed by shallow trenches cut into the turf and backfilled with [[chalk]] rubble.

The origin and age of the figure are unclear, and archaeological evidence suggests that parts of it have been lost, altered, or added, over time; the earliest written record dates to the late 17th century. Early [[antiquarians]] associated it, albeit on little evidence, with a [[Anglo-Saxon paganism|Saxon deity]], while other scholars sought to identify it with a [[Romano-British]] figure of [[Hercules]] (or some [[syncretisation]] of the two).<ref>Rodney Castleden, ''The Cerne Giant'', Dorset Publishing Company, 1996, {{ISBN|978-0948699559}}, pp. 32–33</ref> The lack of earlier descriptions,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hutton |first1=Ronald |title=Queens of the wild: pagan goddesses in Christian Europe an investigation |date=2023 |publisher=Yale University press |location=New Haven (Conn.) London |isbn=9780300273342 |page=23 |quote=In 1983, it was realized that there was no record of the Cerne Abbas Giant before the 17th century, in a valley with good previous records...}}</ref> along with information given to the 18th-century antiquarian [[John Hutchins (antiquary)|John Hutchins]], has led some scholars to conclude it dates from the 17th century. Conversely, recent [[optically stimulated luminescence]] testing has suggested an origin between the years {{CE|700|link=y}} and {{CE|1110}}, possibly close to the 10th-century date of the founding of nearby [[Cerne Abbey]].<ref name="MorcomGittos">{{Cite journal |last1=Morcom |first1=Thomas |last2=Gittos |first2=Helen |date=2024 |title=The Cerne Giant in Its Early Medieval Context |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/727992 |journal=Speculum |language=en |volume=99 |issue=1 |pages=1–38 |doi=10.1086/727992 |s2cid=266375339 |issn=0038-7134|hdl=10852/107522 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Regardless of its age, the Cerne Giant has become an important part of local culture and folklore, which often associates it with [[fertility]]. It is one of England's best-known hill figures and is a visitor attraction in the region.

The Cerne Giant is one of two major extant human hill figures in England, the other being the [[Long Man of Wilmington]], near [[Wilmington, East Sussex]], which is also a scheduled monument.

==Description==
[[File:cerne-abbas-giant-1891-ordnance-survey.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Cerne Abbas Giant on an 1891 [[Ordnance Survey]] map (1:10,560)<ref>"England – Dorset", Ordnance Survey map 1:10,560, Epoch{{nbsp}}1 (1891)</ref>]]

The giant is located just outside the small village of Cerne Abbas in Dorset, about {{convert|30|mile|km|0}} west of [[Bournemouth]] and {{convert|7.5|mile|km|0}} north of [[Dorchester, Dorset|Dorchester]]. The figure depicts a naked man and is of colossal dimensions, being about {{convert|55|m}} long and {{convert|51|m}} across. It is cut into the steep, west-facing side of a hill known as Giant Hill<ref name="heritage">{{NHLE|num=1003202 |desc=Hill figure called The Giant|access-date= 14 October 2012|mode=cs2}}</ref> or Trendle Hill.<ref name="hiddenhistory2009">Haughton, Brian, ''Hidden History: Lost Civilizations, Secret Knowledge, and Ancient Mysteries'', publisher ReadHowYouWant.com, 2009, {{ISBN|978-1442952607}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=AWhGmlxrad0C&q=giant+hill+trendle&pg=PA258 p. 258] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171939/https://books.google.com/books?id=AWhGmlxrad0C&q=giant+hill+trendle&pg=PA258 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref><ref name="holloway">William Holloway, "The Giant of Trendle Hill", The minor minstrel: or, Poetical pieces, chiefly familiar and descriptive, Printed for W. Suttaby, 1808, 182 pages, [https://books.google.com/books?id=UpkuAAAAYAAJ&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PA140 p. 140] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171936/https://books.google.com/books?id=UpkuAAAAYAAJ&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PA140 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> Atop the hill is another landmark, the [[Iron Age Europe|Iron Age]] [[Earthworks (archaeology)|earthwork]] known as the "Trendle" or "Frying Pan".<ref name=hutchins>{{cite book |last=Hutchins |first=John |others=Robert Douch (Contributor) |title=The History and Antiquities of the County of Dorset |orig-year=1742 |year=1973 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield Publishers |location=Oxford |isbn=0874713366 }}</ref> The figure's outline is formed by trenches cut into the turf, about {{convert|0.6|m}} deep, and filled-in with crushed chalk.<ref name="heritage" /> In his right hand, the giant holds a knotted [[Club (weapon)|club]] or baton-style weapon measuring {{convert|37|m}} in length,<ref>Hy. Colley March M.D. F.S.A., "The Giant and the Maypole of Cerne", ''Proceedings'', Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society, Vol. 22, 1901, [https://archive.org/stream/proceedings22dorsuoft#page/108/mode/2up p. 108]</ref> adding {{convert|11|m}} to the total length of the figure.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Piggott|first=Stuart|date=1938|title=The Hercules Myth – beginnings and ends|journal=Antiquity|language=en|volume=12|issue=47|pages=323–31|doi=10.1017/S0003598X00013946|s2cid=163883278 |issn=0003-598X}}</ref> A line across the waist has been suggested to represent a belt.<ref>[[Timothy Darvill]], "[https://books.google.com/books?id=gzEclkBq0u0C&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PT208 Cerne Giant, Dorset, England] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408172023/https://books.google.com/books?id=gzEclkBq0u0C&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PT208 |date=8 April 2023 }}", in ''Concise Oxford Dictionary of Archaeology'', publisher: Oxford University Press, 2009, {{ISBN|978-0199534043}}, 544 pages.</ref> Writing in 1901 in the ''Proceedings'' of the Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society, Henry Colley March noted that: "The Cerne Giant presents five characteristics: (1) It is [[petrographic]]{{nbsp}}... It is, therefore, a [[rock carving]]{{nbsp}}... (2) It is colossal{{nbsp}}... (3) It is nude.{{nbsp}}... (4) It is [[ithyphallic]]{{nbsp}}... (5) The Giant is clavigerous. It bears a weapon in its right hand."<ref>Hy. Colley March M.D. F.S.A., "The Giant and the Maypole of Cerne", ''Proceedings'', Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society, Vol. 22, 1901, [https://archive.org/stream/proceedings22dorsuoft#page/106/mode/2up pp. 107–08]</ref>

A 1996 study found that some features have changed over time, concluding that the figure originally held a cloak over its extended left arm, and an object (possibly a severed head) beneath its left hand.<ref name=Koch395>{{Cite book|last= Koch|first= John T.|title= Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia| publisher= ABC-CLIO|year= 2006|page= 395|isbn=1851094407}}</ref> The former presence of a cloak was corroborated in 2008, when a team of [[archaeologists]] (using special equipment) determined that part of the figure had been lost; the cloak might have been a depiction of an animal skin.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.weymouth.gov.uk/home.asp?sv=295 |title=Cerne Abbas Giant & Cerne Abbas, Dorset |access-date=3 October 2010 |publisher=Weymouth & Portland Borough Council |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090330011530/http://www.weymouth.gov.uk/home.asp?sv=295 |archive-date=30 March 2009 }}</ref> In 1993 the National Trust gave the giant a "nose job" after years of erosion had worn it away.<ref>Chris Court, "Nose Job for Chalk Giant", Press Association, Sunday 11 April 1993, Home News</ref><ref>Raphael Samuel, ''Theatres of Memory: Past and Present in Contemporary Culture'', Publisher: Verso Books, 2012, {{ISBN|978-1844678693}}, 508 pages, [https://books.google.com/books?id=ptjYXlhmyP0C&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PA172 p. 172] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171937/https://books.google.com/books?id=ptjYXlhmyP0C&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PA172 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref>

The giant sports a notably vertical erection, some {{Convert|11|m|abbr=off}} long (nearly the length of its head), along with [[testicle]]s;<ref>Eugene Monick, ''Phallos: Sacred Image of the Masculine'', Volume 27 of Studies in Jungian psychology, publisher Inner City Books, 1987, {{ISBN|978-0919123267}}, 141 pages, [https://books.google.com/books?id=UKKP7wZDSPEC&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PA36 p. 36] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171937/https://books.google.com/books?id=UKKP7wZDSPEC&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PA36 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> it has been called "Britain's most famous [[phallus]]".<ref name="Barnett2000" /> One commentator noted that postcards of the giant were the only indecent photographs "that could be sent through the [[General Post Office|English Post Office]]".<ref name="Editorial">{{cite journal |title=Editorial |journal=Antiquity |date=1976 |volume=50 |issue=198 |pages=89–94 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00070824|doi-access=free }}</ref> However, this feature may also have been changed over time; based on a review of historical depictions, the giant's current large erection has been identified as the result of the merging of a circle (representing his [[navel]]) with a different, smaller [[penis]] during a 1908 re-cut, as the navel still appeared on a late-1890s picture [[postcard]].<ref name="Leslie">{{cite journal |last1=Grinsell |first1=Leslie |title=The Cerne Abbas Giant: 1764–1980 |journal=Antiquity |date=1980 |volume=54 |issue=210 |pages=29–33 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00042824|s2cid=163711386 }}</ref> [[Lidar]] scans, conducted as part of the 2020 survey programme, have concluded that the phallus was added much later than the bulk of the figure, which was (probably) originally clothed.<ref name=telegraph>{{cite news |last=Simpson |first=Craig |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/05/12/rebel-baron-undressed-cerne-abbas-giant-get-rise-oliver-cromwell/ |title=Rebel baron undressed the Cerne Abbas giant to get a rise out of Oliver Cromwell |publisher=Daily Telegraph |date=12 May 2021 |access-date=21 May 2021 |archive-date=21 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210521144900/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/05/12/rebel-baron-undressed-cerne-abbas-giant-get-rise-oliver-cromwell/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The hill figure is most commonly known as the "Cerne Abbas Giant"<ref name="books.google">John Sydenham, ''Baal Durotrigensis. A dissertation on the antient colossal figure at Cerne, Dorsetshire'', London, W. Pickering, 1842. "Section IV" ([https://books.google.com/books?id=Tv8GAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Cerne+Giant%22&pg=PA43 p. 43] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171938/https://books.google.com/books?id=Tv8GAAAAQAAJ&dq=%22Cerne+Giant%22&pg=PA43 |date=8 April 2023 }})</ref><ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/local/dorset/hi/people_and_places/nature/newsid_8571000/8571881.stm "Cerne Abbas Giant: Preserving an icon"], BBC News Dorset, 17 March 2010, retrieved 5 October 2012</ref><ref>"[https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2010/jul/27/cerne-abbas-giant-dorset-fertility Pass notes no 2,820: The Cerne Abbas giant] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313065900/http://www.theguardian.com/travel/2010/jul/27/cerne-abbas-giant-dorset-fertility |date=13 March 2016 }}", The Guardian, 27 July 2010, retrieved 5 October 2012</ref><ref>"[https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sponsored/travel/grand-adventure-holidays/8621225/Visit-the-Cerne-Abbas-Giant-in-Dorset.html Visit the Cerne Abbas Giant in Dorset] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921104127/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sponsored/travel/grand-adventure-holidays/8621225/Visit-the-Cerne-Abbas-Giant-in-Dorset.html |date=21 September 2020 }}", 6 July 2011, retrieved 5 October 2012</ref> or the "Cerne Giant",<ref name="books.google" /><ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cerne-giant/ "Cerne Giant"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120828191927/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cerne-giant/ |date=28 August 2012 }} at the National Trust, retrieved 5 October 2012</ref> the latter being preferred by the National Trust; ==History==

===Early accounts===
Like several other chalk figures carved into the English countryside, the Cerne Abbas Giant is often thought of as an ancient creation but its written history cannot be traced back further than the late 17th century. Medieval sources refer to the hill on which the giant is located as Trendle Hill, in reference to the nearby Iron Age earthwork known as the Trendle.<ref name="hiddenhistory2009" /><ref name=hutchins/> J. H. Bettey of the [[University of Bristol]] noted that none of the earlier sources for the area, including a detailed 1540s survey of the [[Cerne Abbey]] lands and a 1617 land survey by [[John Norden]], refer to the giant, despite noting the Trendle and other landmarks.<ref name="The Cerne Abbas Giant: the document">{{cite journal |last1=Bettey |first1=J. H. |title=The Cerne Abbas Giant: the documentary evidence |journal=Antiquity |date=1981 |volume=55 |issue=214 |pages=118–19 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X0004391X|s2cid=163565157 }}</ref> In contrast, there are documentary references to the 3,000 year-old [[Uffington White Horse]] as far back as the late 11th century.<ref>Martin Symington, ''Sacred Britain: A Guide to Places that Stir the Soul'', publisher: Bradt Travel Guides, 2012, {{ISBN|978-1841623634}}, 240 pages, [https://books.google.com/books?id=KTXOGXztZ-MC&q=cerne+giant+uffington+white+horse&pg=PA53 p. 53] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408172027/https://books.google.com/books?id=KTXOGXztZ-MC&q=cerne+giant+uffington+white+horse&pg=PA53 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref>

The earliest known written reference is a 4{{nbsp}}November 1694 entry in the [[churchwarden's accounts]] from St Mary's Church in Cerne Abbas, which reads "for repairing ye Giant, three shillings".<ref>Katherine Barker, "Brief Encounter: The Cerne Abbas Giantess Project, Summer 1997", ''Proceedings – Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society'', Volume 119, pp. 179–83, citing Vale 1992, ''op.. cit'' [http://research.dorsetcountymuseum.org/c119.html] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120814042804/http://research.dorsetcountymuseum.org/c119.html|date=14 August 2012}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=8tPaAAAAMAAJ&q=cerne+giant+1694] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171940/https://books.google.com/books?id=8tPaAAAAMAAJ&q=cerne+giant+1694|date=8 April 2023}}</ref><ref>Vivian Vale, Patricia Vale, ''Book of Cerne Abbas: Abbey and After'', Halsgrove Press, 2000, {{ISBN|978-1841140698}}</ref> In 1734, the [[Bishop of Bristol]] noted and inquired about the giant during a [[Canonical visitation]] to Cerne Abbas, while in 1738 the antiquarian [[Francis Wise]] mentioned the giant in a letter.<ref>Francis Wise, ''A letter to Dr Mead concerning some antiquities in Berkshire'', printed for Thomas Wood, 1738, [https://books.google.com/books?id=cFAGAAAAQAAJ&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PR90 p. 48] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171944/https://books.google.com/books?id=cFAGAAAAQAAJ&dq=cerne+giant&pg=PR90 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> The bishop's account, as well as subsequent observations such as those of [[William Stukeley]], were discussed at meetings of the [[Society of Antiquaries of London]] in 1764.<ref name=Evans>D. Morgan Evans, "Eighteenth-Century Descriptions of the Cerne Abbas Giant", ''The Antiquaries Journal'', Volume 78, September 1998, [http://journals.cambridge.org/action/displayAbstract?fromPage=online&aid=7853264 p. 463] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131106125729/http://journals.cambridge.org/action/displayAbstract?fromPage=online&aid=7853264 |date=6 November 2013 }} (−471).</ref><ref name="stukeley1764">William Stukeley, ''Minute Book of the Society of Antiquaries'', Vol. IX, p. 233. Thursday 15 March 1764. Reproduced in Hy. Colley March M.D. F.S.A., "The Giant and the Maypole of Cerne", ''Proceedings, Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society'', Vol.22, 1901', [https://archive.org/stream/proceedings22dorsuoft#page/116/mode/2up p. 116].</ref>

Beginning in 1763 descriptions of the giant also began to appear in contemporary magazines, following a general increase in interest in "antiquities". The earliest known survey was published in the ''Royal Magazine'' in September 1763. Derivative versions subsequently appeared in the October 1763 ''St James Chronicle'', the July 1764 ''[[Gentleman's Magazine]]''<ref name=Evans/><ref name="1874gentleman">''The Gentleman's Magazine'', Volume 34, July 1764, [https://books.google.com/books?id=6koDAAAAMAAJ&dq=editions%3AUOM39015018405376&pg=PA336-IA1 p. 336] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171940/https://books.google.com/books?id=6koDAAAAMAAJ&dq=editions%3AUOM39015018405376&pg=PA336-IA1 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> and the 1764 edition of ''[[The Annual Register]]''.<ref name=Evans/><ref>''The Gentleman's magazine'', Volume 34 (August 1764). [https://books.google.com/books?id=6koDAAAAMAAJ&q=giant&pg=PA336 p. 335] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408172032/https://books.google.com/books?id=6koDAAAAMAAJ&q=giant&pg=PA336 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref><ref name=Haughton>{{cite book|title=Hidden History: Lost Civilizations, Secret Knowledge, and Ancient Mysteries|last=Haughton|first=Brian|year=2007|publisher=New Page Books|location=Franklin Lakes, NJ|isbn=978-1564148971|page=[https://archive.org/details/hiddenhistorylos0000haug/page/136 136]|url=https://archive.org/details/hiddenhistorylos0000haug/page/136}}</ref><ref name=Lewis>{{cite news |first=Richard |last=Lewis |title=Celebrating May Day the Pagan Way |url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2005/may/01/unitedkingdom.culturaltrips.observerescapesection1 |newspaper=The Observer |date=1 May 2005 |access-date=20 June 2008 |archive-date=27 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160127124229/http://www.theguardian.com/travel/2005/may/01/unitedkingdom.culturaltrips.observerescapesection1 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>Robert Dodsley, ''The Annual Register'', 1764, [https://books.google.com/books?id=gJlGAAAAcAAJ&q=giant&pg=RA1-PA166 p. 166] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408172027/https://books.google.com/books?id=gJlGAAAAcAAJ&q=giant&pg=RA1-PA166 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> In the early 1770s the antiquarian [[John Hutchins (antiquary)|John Hutchins]] reviewed various previous accounts in his book ''The History and Antiquities of the County of Dorset'', published posthumously in 1774.<ref name=Evans/> Noting a local tradition that the giant had only been cut in the previous century, he described and drew it as then having three roughly-cut letters between its feet, and over them the apparent [[Arabic numerals]] "748", features since lost; Hutchins' account was copied by several early 19th-century guidebooks.<ref>{{cite book |title=The London Encyclopaedia: Or, Universal Dictionary of Science, Art, Literature, and Practical Mechanics, Comprising a Popular View of the Present State of Knowledge. Illustrated by Numerous Engravings, a General Atlas, and Appropriate Diagrams |editor-last=Curtis|editor-first=Thomas |year=1829|publisher=[[Thomas Tegg]]|page=768|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7n9MAAAAMAAJ&q=%22trendle+hill%22&pg=PA290}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Beauties of England and Wales, Or, Delineations, Topographical, Historical, and Descriptive, of Each County |last=Britton|first=John|year=1803|publisher=Thomas Maiden, for Vernor and Hood|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cqQMAAAAIAAJ&q=%22trendle+hill%22&pg=PA483|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

A map referred to as the "1768 Survey Map of Cerne Abbas by Benjamin Pryce" is held at the Dorset History Centre,<ref>"[http://www.cerneabbashistory.org/?page_id=107 Maps & Survey] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130717043806/http://www.cerneabbashistory.org/?page_id=107 |date=17 July 2013 }}", Cerne Abbas Historical Society, retrieved 13 October 2012 ([http://www.cerneabbashistory.org/pdfdocs/1798_SURVEY.pdf illustration] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060348/http://www.cerneabbashistory.org/pdfdocs/1798_SURVEY.pdf |date=21 September 2013 }})</ref> though a record at the National Archives notes there is evidence the map may date to the 1790s.<ref>"Pitt-Rivers Estate Archive, Cerne Abbas map [https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/a2a/records.aspx?cat=031-dpit&cid=4-1-4-2#4-1-4-2 D/PIT/P6?1768-1798] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921054834/https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/a2a/records.aspx?cat=031-dpit&cid=4-1-4-2#4-1-4-2 |date=21 September 2013 }}" at the National Archives, retrieved 13 October 2012</ref> By the following century the phallus was invariably omitted from depictions, either in line with the prevailing views on modesty at the time or as it had become grassed over; the figure seems to have become increasingly neglected and overgrown during the 19th century until in 1868 its owner [[Horace Pitt-Rivers, 6th Baron Rivers|Lord Rivers]] arranged to have the giant restored "as near as possible to his original condition".<ref name=castleden25>Castleden (1996) p.25</ref>

===Interpretation===
18th-century antiquarians were able to discover little about the figure's origin: Stukeley suggested that local people "know nothing more of [the giant] than a traditionary account of its being a deity of the ancient Britons".<ref name=castleden21>Castleden (1996) p.21</ref> Several other local traditions have, however, been recorded, including that the giant was cut in 1539 at the time of the [[dissolution of the monasteries]] as a "humiliating caricature" of Cerne Abbey's final [[abbot]] Thomas Corton, who amongst other offences was accused of fathering children with a mistress.<ref name=harte44>{{cite book |last=Harte |first=Jeremy |title=Cuckoo Pounds and Singing Barrows: The Folklore of Ancient Sites in Dorset |date=1986 |publisher=Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society |page=44}}</ref><ref>Castleden (1996) p.59</ref> Hutchins, noting the apparent figure "748" then visible between the giant's feet, suggested that if this did not refer to the date of an earlier repair such as "1748", it could be a representation of Cenric, the son of [[Cuthred of Wessex]], who died in battle in 748: Arabic numerals however did not come widely into use in England until the 15th century.<ref name=newman82>Newman (2009) p.82</ref> Another 18th-century writer dismissed it as "the amusement of idle people, and cut with little meaning, perhaps, as shepherds' boys strip off the turf on the Wiltshire plains."<ref name=castleden23>Castleden (1996) p.23</ref>

[[Richard Pococke]], in a 1754 account, noted the figure was called "the Giant, and Hele",<ref name="castleden19">Castleden (1996) p. 19</ref> while [[Richard Gough (antiquarian)|Richard Gough]], editor of the 1789 edition of [[William Camden]]'s 1637 work ''Britannica'', linked the giant with a supposed minor [[Anglo-Saxons|Saxon]] deity named by Camden as "Hegle".<ref name=Koch396>{{Cite book|last= Koch|first= John T.|title= Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia| publisher= ABC-CLIO|year= 2006|pages= 395–96|isbn=1851094407}}</ref><ref name=JH1774/> In the 1760s [[William Stukeley]] recorded that locals referred to the giant as "Helis".<ref name=Koch396/> Stukeley was one of the first to hypothesize that "Helis" was a garbled form of "Hercules", a suggestion that has found more support;<ref name=Koch396/><ref>''The modern antiquarian'', Julian Cope, Thorsons 1998</ref> Pococke had earlier noted that "[the giant] seems to be Hercules, or Strength and Fidelity".<ref name="castleden19"/> The close resemblance of the giant's features to the attributes of the classical hero [[Hercules]], usually portrayed naked and with a knotted club, have been strengthened by the more recent discovery of the "cloak", as Hercules was often depicted with the skin of the [[Nemean lion]] over his arm.<ref name=Koch396/>
[[File:Cerne Abbas Giant (obliterated section restored).svg|thumb|Layout of the giant with the obliterated line (in yellow) reconstructed]]
Modern histories of the Cerne Giant have been published by Bettey (1981), [[Rodney Legg|Legg]] (1990), and [[Timothy Darvill|Darvill]] et al. (1999).<ref>"Cerne Abbas", [http://www.dorsetforyou.com/392997 The Dorset Historic Towns Project report on Cerne Abbas] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120903162313/http://www.dorsetforyou.com/392997 |date=3 September 2012 }}, "Part{{nbsp}}3 and{{nbsp}}4 Context and sources (pdf, 492kb)" 4.1 Previous research, p. 21</ref> In recent times there have been three main theories concerning the age of the giant, and whom it might represent:<ref name="Cerne Abbas Giant, Hill-Figure">"[http://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=MNA138903&resourceID=6 Cerne Abbas Giant, Hill-Figure] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131103155455/http://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=MNA138903&resourceID=6 |date=3 November 2013 }}", National Trust Historic Buildings, Sites and Monuments Record (HBSMR) Number 110511, via the English Heritage Gateway, retrieved 30 October 2012</ref>
* One, citing the lack of documentary evidence prior to the 1690s, argues that the giant was created in the 17th century, most likely by [[Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles]], who held the Cerne Abbas estate by right of his second wife Jane. J. H. Bettey was the first to suggest Holles could have cut the figure as a parody of [[Oliver Cromwell]],<ref>"[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cerne-giant/ Cerne Giant] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120828191927/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cerne-giant/ |date=28 August 2012 }}", National Trust website, retrieved 30 October 2012</ref> though a further tradition local to Cerne was that the giant was created by Holles' tenants as a lampoon aimed at Holles himself.<ref>Castleden (1996), p. 46</ref>
* Another, based largely on an idea developed in the 1930s by archaeologist [[Stuart Piggott]], is that due to the giant's resemblance to Hercules, it is a creation of the [[Romano-British culture]], either as a direct depiction of the Roman figure or of a deity identified with him.<ref name=Koch395/> It has been more specifically linked to attempts to revive the cult of Hercules during the reign of the Emperor [[Commodus]] (176-192), who presented himself as a reincarnation of Hercules.<ref>Castleden (1996), p. 97</ref>
* Another is that the giant is of earlier [[Celts|Celtic]] origin, because it is stylistically similar to an image of the Celtic god [[Nodens]] on a [[skillet]] handle found at [[Hod Hill]], Dorset, dated to between 10 CE to 51 CE.<ref name="Cerne Abbas Giant, Hill-Figure"/>

[[File:Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles of Ifield.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles|Lord Holles]], a portrait from the 1640s. Holles, the Cerne Abbas landowner, has been suggested as the person who ordered the giant to be cut in mockery of his political adversary [[Oliver Cromwell|Cromwell]].]]
Proponents of a 17th-century origin suggest that the giant was cut around the time of the [[English Civil War]] by servants of  [[Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles|Denzil Holles]], then [[Lord of the Manor]] of Cerne Abbas. This theory originated in the 18th-century account of John Hutchins, who noted in a letter of 1751 to the Dean of Exeter that the steward of the manor had told him the figure "was a modern thing, cut out in Lord Hollis' time".<ref name=hutchins/> In his ''History and antiquities of the county of Dorset'', first published in 1774, Hutchins also suggested that Holles could perhaps have ordered the recutting of an existing figure dating from "beyond the memory of man".<ref name=JH1774>{{cite book |last1=Hutchins |first1=John |author1-link=John Hutchins (antiquary) |title=The history and antiquities of the county of Dorset |date=1774 |publisher=W. Bowyer and J. Nichols |location=London |oclc=702329446 |volume=2|pages=293–294}}</ref><ref name="sd">{{Cite web |url=http://www.sacred-destinations.com/england/cerne-abbas-giant.htm |title=Cerne Abbas Giant at Sacred Destinations |access-date=2 March 2007 |archive-date=19 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210319032052/https://www.gstatic.com/prose/brandjs.js |url-status=live }}</ref>

It has been speculated that Holles could have intended the figure as a [[parody]] of [[Oliver Cromwell]]: while Holles, the [[Member of parliament|MP]] for [[Dorchester (UK Parliament constituency)|Dorchester]] and a leader of the [[Presbyterian]] faction in Parliament, had been a key [[Roundhead|Parliamentarian]] supporter during the [[First English Civil War]], he grew to personally despise Cromwell and attempted to have him impeached in 1644.<ref name=bcw>[http://bcw-project.org/biography/denzil-holles Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180514205032/http://bcw-project.org/biography/denzil-holles |date=14 May 2018 }}, BCW Project, accessed 10-05-18</ref> Cromwell was sometimes mockingly referred to as "England's Hercules" by his enemies: under this interpretation, the club has been suggested to hint at Cromwell's military rule, and the phallus to mock his [[Puritan]]ism.<ref name=lashmar>Lashmar, "[https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/this-britain/no-prehistoric-giant-step-for-man-but-a-huge-insult-to-cromwell-278918.html No prehistoric giant step for man, but a huge insult to Cromwell] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180513011451/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/this-britain/no-prehistoric-giant-step-for-man-but-a-huge-insult-to-cromwell-278918.html |date=13 May 2018 }}", ''The Independent'', 16-05-2000</ref> In 1967 Kenneth Carrdus proposed that the Holles referred to in Hutchins' account was Denzil Holles' son [[Francis Holles, 2nd Baron Holles|Francis]], MP for Dorchester in 1679-80: he claimed that the figures and letters noted by Hutchins could be made to read "fh 1680", though was unable to find much other evidence to support this.<ref name=castleden49>Castleden (1996) p.49</ref>

The deepest archeological [[Horizon (archaeology)|horizon]] of the giant is 1 metre. Results of [[optically stimulated luminescence]] testing of samples from this deepest level were published in 2021. Some of these samples support a construction date between {{CE|700|link=y}} and {{CE|1110}}, suggesting the giant was first cut in the [[History of Anglo-Saxon England|late Anglo-Saxon period]]. As this date coincides with the founding of nearby Cerne Abbey, archaeologist [[Alison Sheridan]] speculated that it may have been a challenge to the new religion from the still-pagan local inhabitants,<ref name="NT2021" /><ref name="NS">{{cite news |last1=Marshall |first1=Michael |title=Cerne Abbas Giant may have been carved into hill over 1000 years ago |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2277255-cerne-abbas-giant-may-have-been-carved-into-hill-over-1000-years-ago/#ixzz6vCqjDmDo |access-date=18 May 2021 |publisher=[[New Scientist]] |date=12 May 2021 |language=en |archive-date=18 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518003934/https://www.newscientist.com/article/2277255-cerne-abbas-giant-may-have-been-carved-into-hill-over-1000-years-ago/#ixzz6vCqjDmDo |url-status=live }}</ref> although other scholars have noted that early medieval monks could equally have been responsible for the figure.<ref name=raw>Raw, A. "[https://www.theguardian.com/education/2021/may/16/bawdy-monks-and-the-cerne-abbas-giant Bawdy monks and the Cerne Abbas giant] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526171919/https://www.theguardian.com/education/2021/may/16/bawdy-monks-and-the-cerne-abbas-giant |date=26 May 2021 }}", ''The Guardian'', 16-05-21</ref>

Other samples, however, gave later dates ranging up to 1560; one possible explanation is that the giant may have first been cut in the late Saxon period, but then abandoned for several centuries.<ref name=NT2021/> As the survey evidence also suggested that the giant's penis is of much later date than the rest of the figure, the National Trust has proposed that the feature could have been added by Holles as part of his parody of Cromwell when re-cutting the older figure.<ref name=telegraph/>

According to the National Trust, the grass is trimmed regularly and the giant is fully re-chalked every 25 years.<ref>"[https://web.archive.org/web/20110629042803/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-chl/w-countryside_environment/w-archaeology/w-archaeology-places_to_visit/w-archaeology-cerne_abbas_giant.htm ===Archaeology===
[[File:Ercole - Museo archeol. di MI - foto GD'O - 26-6-2003.JPG|thumb|right|Hercules holding a club and the [[Nemean lion]]-skin fur. Roman altar fresco.]]

A 1617 land survey of Cerne Abbas makes no mention of the giant, suggesting that it may not have been there at the time or was perhaps overgrown.<ref name="The Cerne Abbas Giant: the document"/> The first published survey appeared in the September 1763 issue of ''Royal Magazine'', reprinted in the October 1763 issue of ''St James Chronicle'', and also in the August 1764 edition of ''[[Gentleman's Magazine]]'' together with the first drawing that included measurements.<ref name=Evans/>

Egyptologist and archaeology pioneer Sir [[Flinders Petrie]]<ref>Brian Fagan, ''Archaeologists: Explorers of the Human Past'', Oxford University Press, 2003, {{ISBN|978-0195119466}}, 192 pages, [https://books.google.com/books?id=nAfJ1xBD664C&dq=Egyptologist+archaeology+pioneer%2C+Flinders+Petrie&pg=PA72 p. 72] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171946/https://books.google.com/books?id=nAfJ1xBD664C&dq=Egyptologist+archaeology+pioneer%2C+Flinders+Petrie&pg=PA72 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> surveyed the giant, probably during the [[First World War]], and published his results in a [[Royal Anthropological Institute]] paper in 1926.<ref name= Leslie /><ref name="petrie1926">W. M. F. Petrie, ''[http://www.cantab.net/users/michael.behrend/repubs/petrie_hfe/pages/index.html The Hill Figures of England] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131103081237/http://www.cantab.net/users/michael.behrend/repubs/petrie_hfe/pages/index.html |date=3 November 2013 }}'', "III. The Giant of Cerne", Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, Occasional Paper No. 7, 1926</ref> Petrie says he made 220 measurements, and records slight grooves across the neck, and from the shoulders down to the armpits. He also notes a row of pits suggesting the place of the spine. He concludes that the giant is very different from the [[Long Man of Wilmington]], and that minor grooves may have been added from having been repeatedly cleaned.<ref name="petrie1926" />

In 1764, [[William Stukeley]] was one of the first people to suggest that the giant resembled Hercules.<ref name="stukeley1764" /> In 1938, British archaeologist [[Stuart Piggott]] agreed, and suggested that, like Hercules, the giant should also be carrying a lion-skin.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Piggott |first1=Stuart |title=The Hercules Myth – beginnings and ends |journal=Antiquity |date=1938 |volume=12 |issue=47 |pages=323–31 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00013946|s2cid=163883278 }}</ref><ref>Julia De Wolf Addison, ''Classic Myths in Art: An Account of Greek Myths as Illustrated by Great Artists'', Reprinted by Kessinger Publishing, 2003 {{ISBN|978-0766176706}}, 360 pages, [https://books.google.com/books?id=LkCjlir-ITgC&dq=hercules+club+lion+skin+illustrated&pg=PA188 p. 188] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171947/https://books.google.com/books?id=LkCjlir-ITgC&dq=hercules+club+lion+skin+illustrated&pg=PA188 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref> In 1979, a [[resistivity survey]] was carried out, and together with drill samples, confirmed the presence of the lion-skin.<ref>"Cerne Giant", 1979 Resistivity survey by A J Clark, A D H Bartlett and A E U David, English Heritage, [http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1836072 National Monuments Record 1058724] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402114834/http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1836072 |date=2 April 2015 }}</ref> Another resistivity survey in 1995 also found evidence of a cloak and changes to the length of the phallus, but did not find evidence (as rumoured) of a severed head, horns, or symbols between the feet.<ref>"Cerne Giant", 1995 Resistivity survey by A J Clark, A D H Bartlett and A E U David, English Heritage, [http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1870505 1066313] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160127124229/http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1870505 |date=27 January 2016 }}</ref>

In July 2020, preliminary results of a National Trust survey of snail shells unearthed at the site suggested the hill figure is "medieval or later".<ref name="BBC News">{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-dorset-53313064 |title=Cerne Abbas Giant: Snails show chalk hill figure 'not prehistoric' |date=8 July 2020 |work=BBC News |access-date=8 July 2020 |archive-date=8 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200708010212/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-dorset-53313064 |url-status=live }}</ref> Snails dating only from the Roman period (brought from France as food) were not found at the site, while species first found in England from the 13th and 14th centuries were found in soil samples examined. In 2020 the National Trust commissioned a further survey, using [[optically stimulated luminescence]], and the results contradicted earlier research and theories. Samples from inside the deepest layers of the monument yielded a date range for construction of {{CE|700–1100}}{{snd}} early medieval late [[Anglo-Saxon]] period.<ref name=NT2021>{{cite web |title=National Trust archaeologists surprised by likely age of Cerne Abbas Giant |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cerne-giant/news/national-trust-archaeologists-surprised-by-likely-age-of-cerne-abbas-giant- |website=National Trust |access-date=12 May 2021 |language=en |archive-date=11 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210511234737/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cerne-giant/news/national-trust-archaeologists-surprised-by-likely-age-of-cerne-abbas-giant- |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Kindy|first=David|title=Scholars Are One Step Closer to Solving the Mystery of an Enormous Chalk Figure|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scholars-are-one-step-closer-solving-mystery-enormous-chalk-figure-180977725/|access-date=2021-05-17|website=Smithsonian Magazine|language=en|archive-date=17 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517112525/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scholars-are-one-step-closer-solving-mystery-enormous-chalk-figure-180977725/|url-status=live}}</ref> The discovery was featured in Series 9, Episode 5 of the BBC series ''[[Digging for Britain]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m0013f61|title=BBC Two - Digging for Britain, Series 9, Episode 5|website=BBC}}</ref>

A 2024 study proposed that the figure depicts Hercules and was created {{Circa|900}} CE as a [[Muster (military)|muster station]] for [[Wessex|West Saxon]] armies to gather and that by the 11th-century, the figure was being reinterpreted as portraying [[Saint Eadwold]], by the monks at the Abbey.<ref name="MorcomGittos"/>

====Earthworks====
North-east of the head of the giant is an escarpment called Trendle Hill, on which are some earthworks now called The Trendle or Frying Pan.<ref name="NTADStrendle">"[http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1784533 The Trendle, Possible Roman Rectangular Earthwork Enclosure] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304002033/http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1784533 |date=4 March 2016 }}", National Trust Archaeological Data Service</ref> It is a scheduled monument in its own right.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1002725 |desc=Earthworks on Giant Hill|access-date=25 October 2012|mode=cs2}}</ref> Antiquarian John Hutchins wrote in 1872 that "These remains are of very interesting character, and of considerable extent. They consist of circular and other earthworks, lines of defensive ramparts, an avenue, shallow excavations, and other indications of a British settlement."<ref>Hutchins (1742), quoted in Dr Wake Smart, "The Cerne Giant", ''Journal of the British Archaeological Association'', Volume: 28, 1872, [https://archive.org/stream/journalofbritish28brit#page/64/mode/2up p. 65]</ref>

Unlike the giant, the earthworks belong to [[Lord Digby]], rather than the National Trust. Its purpose is unknown; the claim that it was the site of [[maypole dancing]], made by the former village [[Sexton (office)|sexton]] in the late 19th century, was disputed by other villagers who located the maypole site elsewhere.<ref name=harte45>Harte (1986), pp. 45-46</ref><ref name="NTADStrendle" /> It has been considered to be Roman,<ref name="NTADStrendle" /> or perhaps an Iron-Age burial mound containing the tomb of the person represented by the giant.<ref>James Dyer, ''Southern England: an archaeological guide'', publisher Noyes Press, 1973, pp. 81–82</ref><ref>{{PastScape|mnumber=199018 |mname=The Trendle|access-date= 25 October 2012}}</ref>

==Folklore==
Whatever its origin, the giant has become an important part of the culture and folklore of Dorset. Some folk stories indicate that the image is an outline of the corpse of a real giant.<ref name=Koch396/> One story says the giant came from [[Denmark]] leading an invasion of the coast, and was beheaded by the people of Cerne Abbas while he slept on the hillside.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Social Circulation of the Past: English Historical Culture 1500–1730 |last=Woolf |first=Daniel R. |year=2003 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0199257787 |page=348, footnote 178 }}</ref>

In 1808 Dorset poet William Holloway published his poem "The Giant of Trendle Hill", in which the giant is killed by the locals by piercing its heart.<ref name="holloway" />

Other folklore, first recorded in the [[Victorian era]], associates the figure with fertility.<ref name=Koch396/> According to folk belief, a woman who sleeps on the figure will be blessed with [[fecundity]], and infertility may be cured through sexual intercourse on top of the figure, especially the phallus.<ref name=Koch396/>

===Representations===
In 1980, Devon artist Kenneth Evans-Loud planned to produce a companion {{Convert|70|m|adj=on}} female figure on the opposite hill, featuring [[Marilyn Monroe]] in her iconic pose from the film ''[[The Seven Year Itch]]'' where her dress is blown away by the blast coming from a subway grate.<ref>Annabel Ferriman, "Objections to hill figure", ''The Times'', issue No. 60571, 10 March 1980, p. 2.</ref><ref>Rodney Castleden, ''The Cerne Giant'', Dorset Publishing Company, 1996, {{ISBN|978-0948699559}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=du2fAAAAMAAJ&q=%22kenneth+evans-loude%22 p. 37] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230408171943/https://books.google.com/books?id=du2fAAAAMAAJ&q=%22kenneth+evans-loude%22 |date=8 April 2023 }}</ref>

In 1989, Turner Prize-winning artist [[Grayson Perry]] designed a set of motorbike leathers inspired by the Cerne Abbas Giant.<ref>Naomi West, [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/3663237/The-world-of....html "The world of{{nbsp}}..."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180704105032/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/3663237/The-world-of....html |date=4 July 2018 }}, ''The Telegraph'', 17 February 2007, retrieved 11 October 2012</ref><ref>"Grayson Perry at the British Museum", ''The Vintage'', 15 December 2011</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20121011223343/http://londonersdiary.standard.co.uk/2011/03/saucy-tips-for-the-ladies-who-lunch.html "Saucy tips for the ladies who lunch"], ''London Evening Standard'', 10 March 2011, retrieved 11 October 2012</ref> In 1994, girls from [[Roedean School]] painted a {{convert|24|m|adj=on}} replica of the giant on their playing field, the day before sports day.<ref>Jack O'Sullivan, [https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/so-you-still-want-to-send-the-kids-to-boarding-school-1081328.html "So you still want to send the kids to boarding school?"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180704151713/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/so-you-still-want-to-send-the-kids-to-boarding-school-1081328.html |date=4 July 2018 }}, ''The Independent'', 18 March 1999, retrieved 12 October 2012</ref>

In 2003, pranksters created their own {{convert|23|m|adj=on}} version of the giant on a hill in [[English Bicknor]], Gloucestershire, but "wearing wellies, an ear of corn hanging from its mouth and a tankard of ale in its hand".<ref>[http://www.accessmylibrary.com/coms2/summary_0286-23020884_ITM "Pranksters Create A Naked Giant Imposter"], ''Western Daily Press'', 15 April 2003, p. 23</ref> In 2005, the makers of Lynx deodorant created a {{convert|9.3|m2|sqft|sigfig=4}} advert on a field near [[Gatwick Airport]], featuring a copy of the giant wearing underpants, frolicking with two scantily clad women.<ref>"Huge deodorant advert washed away", ''BBC News'', 26 July 2005</ref> In 2006, artist Peter John Hardwick produced a painting "The Two Dancers with the Cerne Abbas Giant, with Apologies to [[Picasso]]" which is on display at [[Poole Hospital]] NHS Foundation Trust.<ref>Peter John Hardwick, [https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/the-two-dancers-with-the-cerne-abbas-giant-with-apologies-to-picasso-59905 "The Two Dancers with the Cerne Abbas Giant, with Apologies to Picasso"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200428174206/https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/the-two-dancers-with-the-cerne-abbas-giant-with-apologies-to-picasso-59905 |date=28 April 2020 }}, ''BBC Your Paintings'', retrieved 12 October 2012</ref> In 2009, the giant was given a red nose, to publicize the BBC's Comic Relief charity event.<ref>"Cerne Abbas Giant given red nose", ''BBC News Dorset'', 12 February 2009, retrieved 12 October 2012</ref> In 2011, English animators [[The Brothers McLeod]] produced a 15-second cartoon giving their take on what the giant does when no one is watching.<ref>The Brothers McLeod, [https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p00krgw1 "Funny in 15: Cerne Abbas"], 29 September 2011, retrieved 12 October 2012</ref>

In 2015, the giant was used as a character in an online comic book published by Eco Comics; the giant's character appeared in various adventures accompanying a character based on [[St George]], though his erect penis was removed from the artwork as many "outlets, particularly in the US, refuse any form of nudity in comic books".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/newstopics/howaboutthat/11591904/Giant-chalk-hillside-figure-in-Cerne-Abbas-censored-for-American-audience.html |title=Giant chalk hillside figure in Cerne Abbas censored for American audience |publisher=Telegraph Media Group Limited |first=Victoria |last=Ward |date=8 May 2015 |access-date=8 May 2015 |archive-date=10 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150510211827/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/newstopics/howaboutthat/11591904/Giant-chalk-hillside-figure-in-Cerne-Abbas-censored-for-American-audience.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The giant's image has been reproduced on various souvenirs and local food produce labels, including for a range of beers made by the Cerne Abbas Brewery. In 2016, the [[BBC]] reported that the beer company's logo had been censored in the [[Houses of Parliament]].<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-dorset-35502433 "Cerne Abbas giant beer logo censored in Parliament bar"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180531044618/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-dorset-35502433 |date=31 May 2018 }}, ''BBC News'', 5 February 2016, retrieved 29 July 2017</ref>

54565442.title: Parke, Bovey Tracey
54565442.extract: Parke is an historic estate in the parish of Bovey Tracey in Devon, England. The present mansion house known as Parke House, a grade II listed building  situated 1/2 mile west of the centre of the town of Bovey Tracey and on the opposite side of the River Bovey, was rebuilt in 1826/8 by William Hole (1799-1859) and is today the headquarters of the Dartmoor National Park Authority.

main.*:
{{Short description|Historic estate in Devon, England}}
[[File:Parke House, Bovey Tracey - geograph.org.uk - 1418812.jpg|thumb|Parke House in 2009, as rebuilt in 1826/8 by William Hole (1799-1859)]]
'''Parke''' is an historic estate in the parish of [[Bovey Tracey]] in Devon, England. The present mansion house known as '''Parke House''', a [[Listed building|grade II listed]] building<ref>[http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101096646-parke-house-including-the-stables-bovey-tracey#.WWvXw1GQwqc Listed building text]</ref>  situated 1/2 mile west of the centre of the town of Bovey Tracey<ref name="Pevsner, p.193">Pevsner, p.193</ref> and on the opposite side of the [[River Bovey]], was rebuilt in 1826/8 by William Hole (1799-1859) and is today{{When|date=July 2022}} the headquarters of the [[Dartmoor National Park]] Authority.

==Descent==

===Eveleigh===
Parke was the seat of [[Nicholas Eveleigh (died 1618)]],<ref>Gatehouse gazetteer</ref> a [[junior barrister]], who served as Steward of the Stannary Court of Ashburton, Devon.<ref>As stated in the lawsuit ''Foster v Courteney'' heard in the Star Chamber in June 1608, recorded in STAC 8/142/11, National Archives, Kew [http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C5571175]</ref> He died aged 56 when the roof of Chagford Stannary Courthouse collapsed, killing him and nine others. His "sumptuous"<ref>Pevsner, p.191</ref> monument with an effigy survives in Bovey Tracey Church.

===Hele===
Eveleigh's  widow married  the lawyer [[Elize Hele]] (1560–1635)<ref>[[John Lambrick Vivian|Vivian, Lt.Col. J.L.]], (Ed.) The Visitations of the County of Devon: Comprising the  [[Heraldic visitation|Heralds' Visitations]] of 1531, 1564 & 1620, Exeter, 1895, p.467, pedigree of Hele</ref> (also seated at [[Fardel, Cornwood|Fardel]]<ref>[[John Prince (biographer)|Prince, John]], (1643–1723) The Worthies of Devon, 1810 edition, London, p.487; also as inscribed on his [[ledger stone]] in [[Exeter Cathedral]], as recorded in Prince, p.488</ref> in the parish of [[Cornwood]], Devon), who  founded [[Plympton Grammar School]]<ref>Inscribed bronze plaque near building</ref> (''alias'' [[Hele's School]]). An elaborate monument with an effigy to Elize Hele survives in Bovey Tracey Church, facing that of Eveleigh.

===Stawell===
[[File:StawellArms.png|thumb|150px|Arms of Stawell]]

Sir John Stawell (1625-1669) of Parke, a counsellor-at-law.<ref>Per [[History of Parliament]] biography of his son [[William Stawell (MP)|William Stawell]] [http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1660-1690/member/stawell-william-1651-1702#footnote2_8ut53ap]</ref> In 1653 he purchased [[Torre Abbey]], Torquay.<ref>Rhodes, Michael, ''Devon's Torre Abbey: Faith, Politics and Grand Designs'', Stroud, Gloucestershire, 2015, p.65</ref> He married Sarah Stephens, a daughter of Nathaniel Stephens (1589–1660), of Eastington in Gloucestershire, twice a [[Member of Parliament]] for [[Gloucestershire (UK Parliament constituency)|Gloucestershire]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1604-1629/member/stephens-nathaniel-1589-1660|title=STEPHENS, Nathaniel (1589-1660), of Eastington, Glos. | History of Parliament Online}}</ref> He had at least three sons, the eldest of whom, William Stawell (c.1651-1702), MP, erected a mural monument to his father and younger brother in Bovey Tracey Church.

William Stawell (c. 1651 – 1702), son and heir, of Parke, was elected nine-times a [[Member of Parliament]] for [[Ashburton (UK Parliament constituency)|Ashburton]] in Devon,<ref>[[History of Parliament]] biography of "STAWELL, William (c.1651-1702), of Parke, Bovey Tracey, Devon"[http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1660-1690/member/stawell-william-1651-1702]</ref> due to his patronage derived from his ownership of a [[Moiety title|moiety]] of the manor and borough of Ashburton. He died unmarried.

===(Dunning)===
Pevsner suggests that Parke, Bovey Tracey, was a seat of the prominent lawyer and politician [[John Dunning, 1st Baron Ashburton]] (1731–1783),<ref name="Pevsner, p.193" /> but he appears to have confused it with a farmhouse called "Park" (7 miles south-west of Parke, Bovey Tracey) within his manor of [[Widecombe-in-the-Moor]] on [[Dartmoor]], to which shortly after his acquisition of that manor he had "added a room or two".<ref>[[Todd Gray (Devon Historian)|Gray, Todd]] & Rowe, Margery (Eds.), Travels in Georgian Devon: The Illustrated Journals of The Reverend [[John Swete]], 1789-1800, 4 vols., Tiverton, 1999, Vol.1, pp.102-3. Swete notes that at the time of his visit to Sandridge in the company of Sir Robert Palk, his host was then plain "Mr Dunning", placing the date before 1782 (a year before his death) when he was raised to the peerage, but also long before the building of the mansion at Park</ref> This farmhouse he enlarged and transformed into a house called [[Spitchwick]] Park (to be distinguished also from Stickwick near Hennock, 2 miles north-east of Bovey Tracy, a seat of the Hole family).

===Clapp===
[[File:GeorgeHuntClapp Died1824 BoveyTraceyChurch Devon.PNG|thumb|Mural monument to George Hunt Clapp (1756-1824), Bovey Tracey Church]]
It was the seat of George Hunt Clapp (1756-1824), a barrister and a bencher of the [[Middle Temple]], and in 1798 a governor for life of the [[Magdalen Hospital]] in London.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=_QxeAAAAcAAJ&dq=George+Hunt+Clapp+middle+temple&pg=PA10 A List of the Governors of the Magdalen Hospital, 1798]</ref> His inscribed mural monument survives in Bovey Tracey Church. His origins are revealed by the will of his grandfather George Hunt (d.1768) of Northwick, signed 31 October 1766. He leaves all his freehold lands and tenements in the parishes of North Bovey and Throwleigh, immediately upon his own decease, to "my grandson George Luxton, son of Thomas Luxton and Elizabeth his wife, my daughter, of Winkleigh, Esq.," with 
remainders to " my granddaughter Elizabeth Luxton, sister of the said G. L.," and "my granddaughter Mary Luxton, younger sister of the said G. L." He leaves Tarr Mill in S. T., immediately after his decease, to "my grandson George Hunt Clapp, son of Robert Clapp and Mary his wife, my youngest daughter, of Ottery St. Mary, gent.," with remainders to " my grandson Francis Hunt Clapp," and others.<ref>Devon and Cornwall Notes and Queries, Volume IX, (January 1916 to October 1917), p.24 [https://archive.org/stream/devoncornwallnot09amer/devoncornwallnot09amer_djvu.txt]</ref>

===Hole===
[[File:HoleArms.png|thumb|Arms of Hole: ''Azure, an annulet argent between three lozenges or'']]

====William Hole (1799-1859)====
[[File:Monument WilliamHole Died1779 BoveyTraceyChurch Devon.PNG|thumb|Monument in Bovey Tracey Church to William Hole (1701-1779) of Crownley, Bovey Tracey, grandfather of the rebuilder of Parke House]]
William Hole (1799-1859) of Stickwick (in the parish of Bovey Tracey, 2 miles north-east of that town), purchased the nearby estate of Parke in 1825.<ref name="Heritage Gateway - Results">{{Cite web|url=http://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=MDV30583&resourceID=104|title = Heritage Gateway - Results}}</ref> He was the only son and heir of Robert Hole (1742-1822) who built Stickwick in 1780-2,<ref>"The original building account for Stickwick survives, showing that Robert Hole 'begun to lay the foundation' on 18 May 1780; most of the work was completed by January 1782, but the final bill was not paid
until 25 October 1785. Chimneypieces were provided by Mr Robinson of Chudleigh. The parlour and parlour chamber were hung with paper. The roof was slated from the first. Lime ashes were used for the floors. Cost £591-10-8" (Listed building text [http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101097423-stickwick-house-and-farmhouse-bovey-tracey#.WWwEGFGQwqc])</ref> (son of William Hole (1701-1779) of Crownley, in the parish of Bovey Tracey, by his wife Anne Blatchford, daughter of Theophilus Blatchford) by his wife Anne Pitts (d.1809), a daughter of Joseph Pitts of Kiln in the parish of [[Drewsteignton]], Devon.<ref>[[John Burke (genealogist)|
Burke's]] Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Landed Gentry, 15th Edition, ed. Pirie-Gordon, H., London, 1937, p.1137, pedigree of ''Hole of Parke''</ref> He was educated at Harrow and in 1822 married Susan Kitson (d.1895), eldest daughter of Rev. William Kitson, of Shiphay, Devon.<ref name="BLG, 1937, p.1137">BLG, 1937, p.1137</ref> In 1826/28<ref name="Heritage Gateway - Results" /> he demolished the ancient house at Parke and rebuilt it as the present surviving house.<ref>[[Nikolaus Pevsner|Pevsner, Nikolaus]] & Cherry, Bridget, The Buildings of England: Devon, London, 2004, p.193</ref>

====William Robert Hole (1831-1903)====
William Robert Hole (1831-1903), [[Justice of the Peace]], [[Deputy Lieutenant]],<ref name="BLG, 1937, p.1137" /> only son, a [[Chartered Accountant]],<ref>"CA", BLG, 1937, p.1137</ref> whose portrait is in the collection of the National Trust.<ref>[http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1296517 See image]</ref> He was educated at Winchester and Eton. In 1875 he married Laetitia Parlby, a daughter of Rev. John Hall [[Thomas Parlby|Parlby]], JP, of [[Manadon]], near [[Plymouth]].<ref name="BLG, 1937, p.1137" /> He died in a horse-riding accident on 7 February 1903. In 1905 his widow presented a stained glass window to Bovey Tracey Church in his memory, depicting the [[Resurrection]], forming the east window of the [[Lady Chapel]].<ref name="framed note">Framed note in church</ref>

====William Gerald Hole (1881-1974)====
Major William Gerald Hole (1881-1974), son, who was educated at Winchester and [[Merton College, Oxford]].<ref name="MCreg">{{cite book|editor1-last=Levens|editor1-first=R.G.C.|title=Merton College Register 1900–1964|date=1964|publisher=Basil Blackwell|location=Oxford|page=20}}</ref> He served in the Devon Imperial Yeomanry (Royal 1st Devon Yeomanry<ref name="BLG, 1937, p.1137" />) at Gallipoli and in Palestine during [[World War I]]. In 1905 he married Mildred Bingley, daughter of Rev. John Bingley of Woodford, Torquay, by whom he had an only daughter and sole heiress (Mildred) Geraldine Hole (1908-2008),<ref name="BLG, 1937, p.1137" /> who in 1939 married Fleetwood Hugo Pellew (1910-2008) of Coppelia House, Moreton Hampstead,<ref>{{Cite web | title=PELLEW, EXMOUTH - Family Ancestry and Descendants Page No 2 | url=https://www.pellew.com/Family%20Tree/Family%20Tree.htm#9th%20Viscount%20Exmouth%202 | access-date=2025-03-20 | website=www.pellew.com}}</ref> Devon (2nd cousin of [[Pownoll Irving Edward Pellew, 9th Viscount Exmouth]] (1908–1970)), and left one daughter. William Gerald Hole presented a stained glass window to Bovey Tracey Church depicting the [[Road to Emmaus appearance|Road to Emmaus]], forming the south window of the [[Lady Chapel]].<ref name="framed note" />

He bequeathed the Parke estate, comprising the house and 239 acres, to the National Trust.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1296517|title=William Robert Hole (1831-1903) 1296517}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/ |title=Home |website=heritagegateway.org.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://adriancolston.wordpress.com/tag/william-hole/|title = William Hole}}</ref>

Several inscribed mural monuments to the Hole family of Parke, Stickwick and Crownley, survive in Bovey Tracey Church, also the east and south windows of the Lady Chapel, donated by the family.

===Dartmoor National Park Authority===
The mansion house of Parke is today leased to [[Devon County Council]]<ref name="Heritage Gateway - Results" /> as the headquarters of the [[Dartmoor National Park]] Authority.<ref name="Pevsner, p.193" />

'''Plymbridge Woods''' is a woodland in [[Plympton]], Devon, England managed by [[The National Trust]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/plymbridge-woods|title=Plymbridge Woods|website=National Trust}}</ref> The woods are named after the historic Plymbridge, a Grade II listed bridge over the [[River Plym]]. Drake's Trail passes through the woods providing a cycling and walking route. There is a range of wildlife, birds and flora.

==History==
[[File:Plymbridge (9492).jpg|thumb|right|200px|Plymbridge]]
[[File:Cycle track in plymbridge woods - panoramio.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Drake's Trail]]
The woodland is named after Plymbridge a historic bridge over the [[River Plym]] which is Grade II listed with [[Historic England]].<ref name="auto">{{NHLE|num=1162902|desc=PLYM BRIDGE, Non Civil Parish |accessdate=25 September 2018}}</ref> A bridge has existed at this location from as early as 1238 with the current bridge being circa 18th century but seated on earlier [[Pier (architecture)|piers]]. It is made from [[Killas]] rubble with five semi-circular arches having [[parapets]] with chamfered granite coping stones.<ref name="auto"/>

A number of tram and railway lines were constructed to transport granite and slate between [[Dartmoor]] and [[Plymouth]]. The last line to be built was the [[South Devon and Tavistock Railway]] upon which [[Isambard Kingdom Brunel]] worked. It was taken over by the [[Great Western Railway]] and closed in 1962. It is now called Drake's Trail and is used as a footpath and cycle route through the woodland. There are remains of the quarrying history including the shell of old buildings used by families involved in the industry. Most quarries in the area were used to mine slate, which was abundant. A section of the trail passes Cann Viaduct.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/devon/outdoors/walks/plymbridge_woods.shtml|title=BBC - Devon Great Outdoors - Walks - Plym Bridge Woods|website=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref>

==Nature==
The site is home to many species typical of English woodland, including a herd of [[fallow deer]]. There are [[goosander]]s, [[mandarin duck]]s, [[kingfishers]] and [[dipper]]s along the river. [[Peregrine falcons]] have nested in Cann Quarry since the 1960s and since 2002 the National Trust have maintained a watchpoint, staffed by volunteers, on Cann Viaduct from which it is usually possible to see the nest site. The site supports damselflies and butterflies.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.visitplymouth.co.uk/things-to-do/plymbridge-woods-p182823|title=Plymbridge Woods - Country Park/Nature Reserve in Plymouth, Plymouth - Visit Plymouth|website=www.visitplymouth.co.uk}}</ref>

==Recreation==
The woods are used for walking, cycling, dog walking and viewing the natural flora and fauna. Plymvalley [[Parkrun]] takes place in the woods starting at Plymbridge.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.parkrun.org.uk/plymvalley/course/|title=Course - Plymvalley parkrun|website=www.parkrun.org.uk}}</ref> The National Trust has a permanent [[orienteering]] course and a mountain bike trail in the woods<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.britishorienteering.org.uk/poc/plymbridge_woods_nt|title=British Orienteering|website=www.britishorienteering.org.uk}}</ref> and the [[Devon Coast to Coast Cycle Route]] runs through the woods.
